new_statements.quote: Tiba has a three-level tone system, complicated by downstep and grammatical tone alternation. Downstep occurs automatically (as a mere phonetic realization) after a rising (LH) contour tone. It also occurs syntactically (i.e., as a mark of certain syntactic relationships without necessarily requiring postulation of any "underlying" (deleted) L tone), and as a "surface" phenomenon, i.e., where the deletion of an underlying tone may be supposed. [...] NOUN TONE CLASSES: Note that about one half of all nominals have a HM or H tone pattern; another quarter has MH or M. Other fairly well represented nominal root tone patterns are LH, LHM, HL(M), and L.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The language is described as a three-level (H, M, L) tone language with downstep and grammatical tone alternation; lexical tone patterns are listed for nouns and verbs. The words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur in a phonological sense anywhere in the 65-page sketch.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (none stated). For tone: downstep after LH contours; H/HM nouns change tone when modified; verb tone classes hard to establish from the elicitation context.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone (nouns, verbs) plus syntactic downstep; data from one informant, elicited via Chamba Daka (the author calls the description provisional).
new_statements.identity_note: Boyd 1999 describes 'Tiba (Gà)' from one speaker at Gambe near Pola, Adamawa State, Nigeria; autonym per Boyd 'Gà(ã)'; this is the gaaa1245 language (Glottolog, PHOIBLE and Grambank all attach Boyd 1999 to gaaa1245). Boyd argues it is Adamawa (Mumuye-Yendang) heavily relexified from Chamba Daka, against the Ethnologue/Glottolog Dakoid placement. The Glottolog ref Djouonzo 2005 'Nom en Təbaya (Tiba)' is a Yaoundé thesis on Tibea (tibe1274, Cameroon) and almost certainly not this language.
